passage: Zubin, come, sit. I am Ritu, your Masi, and I want to tell you about the day I was nine. My teacher read my spelling test aloud, laughed and said, "Is this an elephant's handwriting?" The whole class giggled. I wanted to vanish under the desk. I did not eat that night. When my mother asked, I told her. She did not say I was too sensitive. She said, "You did nothing to deserve that," and the next morning she and my father went to speak to the principal. The teacher never mocked anyone again. I have never forgotten that my mother believed me.

qa.q: What did the teacher say about Ritu's handwriting?
qa.a: The teacher said, "Is this an elephant's handwriting?"

qa.q: What did nine-year-old Ritu want to do when the class giggled?
qa.a: She wanted to vanish under the desk, which shows how ashamed she felt.

qa.q: What did Ritu's mother do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She listened, said Ritu had done nothing to deserve it and went to the principal with Ritu's father, so Ritu knew she was believed and the school heard about it.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel hearing Masi Ritu's story?
qa.a: Zubin may feel less alone and more willing to tell a parent if a teacher ever shames Zubin.

grounding: An elder recalls being mocked by a teacher, telling her parents and their raising it with the school; adults should correct, not shame.

passage: In the English period, Yamini read her poem aloud, and her voice wobbled on the word 'butterfly'. The teacher smirked. 'Did everyone hear our little opera singer?' The class laughed. Yamini stared at her desk and wished the floor would open. Hansa, beside her, squeezed her hand under the table. At lunch Yamini couldn't eat. 'That was mean of her,' Hansa said. 'Not your fault. Tell your mum today.' That evening Yamini told Amma everything, her voice small. Amma listened without interrupting, then hugged her. 'A teacher should correct you, never shame you. That was wrong.' Before dinner, Amma wrote to the principal asking for a meeting, and read the message to Yamini before sending it.

qa.q: Which word did Yamini's voice wobble on?
How did Yamini feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: Humiliated and ashamed; she wished the floor would open and couldn't eat at lunch.

qa.q: What did Amma do that same evening?
qa.a: Listened, said it was wrong and not Yamini's fault, and wrote to the principal asking for a meeting.

qa.q: How did Hansa see what the teacher did?
qa.a: As mean and unfair; Hansa squeezed Yamini's hand and urged Yamini to tell her mum.

grounding: A girl mocked by a teacher in class tells her mother, who says it was wrong and raises it with the school the same evening.

passage:
Monday. In PE, Aditi dropped the ball twice, and Ms Kapoor shouted, 'Look, everyone, butterfingers strikes again!' and made her stand at the side for the rest of the game. Some kids laughed. Aditi wanted to disappear into the ground. At home she said nothing and went to bed early.
Tuesday. Mumma found her crying over her PE shoes. Aditi told her. Mumma's jaw set. 'Being mocked like that is not okay. It's not your fault.' She called the school that same morning.
Wednesday. Mumma and Papa met the counsellor, Mrs Chandrika Rao, and the principal. That afternoon Ms Kapoor took Aditi aside and said sorry. 'I was wrong to embarrass you.' Aditi still felt shaky in PE, but she caught the ball once.

qa.q: What did Ms Kapoor call Aditi?
What was Aditi feeling on Monday night?
qa.a: Humiliated and ashamed; she said nothing and went to bed early.

qa.q: What did Aditi's parents do once they knew?
qa.a: Mumma said it wasn't her fault and called the school; the next day the parents met the counsellor and the principal.

qa.q: What might Ms Kapoor have felt when she said sorry?
qa.a: Perhaps embarrassed and regretful after realising she had shamed Aditi.

grounding: Over three days a girl shamed by a teacher in front of the class tells her mother, and her parents raise it with the school.
